meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The thing about smart people is that they seem like crazy people to dumb people'?
meta.ogDescription: Hawking never said it. The earliest citation is a 4 Nov 2011 tweet with no author, and a 2012 skeptics' book quotes it as an anonymous comment.

answer.label: Not Stephen Hawking — an anonymous internet saying
answer.authorName: Unknown — anonymous; circulating online by November 2011
answer.authorDates: No documented author · earliest citation on record: 4 November 2011
answer.sourceLine: There is no source for this line in Stephen Hawking’s work. It appears in none of his books, lectures or documented interviews, and Wikiquote’s Hawking page ↗ does not carry it in any section — not under Quotes, not even under Attributed or Misattributed. Quotation researcher Barry Popik ↗, who compiled the citation record for this saying, states plainly that there is no evidence Hawking originated it or even said it: the earliest citation he lists is an unattributed Twitter post of 4 November 2011, and the first post crediting Hawking does not appear until 7 October 2013.

source.excerpt: One commenter posted the following: “The thing about smart people is that they seem like crazy people to dumb people.”
trail: Barry Popik’s entry ↗ for this exact saying states there is no evidence Stephen Hawking originated it or said it. The earliest citation he lists is a Twitter post of 4 November 2011 carrying the line with no author; the following day another user posted it credited to “Unknown author.”

The same record dates the first Hawking credit to a Twitter post of 7 October 2013 ↗, with further Hawking-credited posts in April 2014 and after. Hawking was alive at the time and died on 14 March 2018; no source in his own words has ever surfaced.
Wikiquote’s Stephen Hawking page ↗ does not carry the line anywhere — not in the sourced Quotes section, and not in its Attributed or Misattributed sections either.

A structurally similar but far coarser line, spoken by Abraham, appears in Robert Kirkman and Charlie Adlard’s The Walking Dead, Vol. 9: Here We Remain ↗, published 7 January 2009 ↗. The wording differs and no researcher has linked the two, so we note it as a parallel rather than a source.
source.cutTag: the earliest book citation — an anonymous comment, not a Hawking quote
source.excerptNote: Robert Todd Carroll, Unnatural Acts: Critical Thinking, Skepticism, and Science Exposed! (2012), p. 138, as transcribed in Barry Popik’s citation record ↗. This is the earliest book appearance on record, and it treats the line for exactly what it was — an anonymous online comment. It was published a year before anyone credited Stephen Hawking.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording has no identified author and no identified first publication — the earliest citation on record is an anonymous 2011 Twitter post — so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. The texts that quote it are separate works and remain in copyright: Robert Todd Carroll’s Unnatural Acts (2011–2012) and Robert Kirkman’s The Walking Dead, Vol. 9 (2009), neither of which is the saying itself.

author.name: Stephen Hawking
author.kicker: The name it got pinned to
author.heading: About Stephen Hawking
author.metaLine: 1942–2018 · English theoretical physicist & cosmologist, Lucasian Professor at Cambridge 1979–2009
author.bio: Stephen Hawking was an English theoretical physicist and cosmologist, born in Oxford on 8 January 1942 and Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge from 1979 to 2009. His A Brief History of Time (1988) sold in the millions and made him the most recognisable scientist alive, a status that also made him one of the internet’s favourite hosts for unsourced aphorisms. He died on 14 March 2018 — more than four years after this particular line was first pinned on him, and it has never been found anywhere in his own words.

cite.sourceCitation: The earliest citation in Barry Popik’s record for this saying is an unattributed Twitter post by @SecularAdvocate, 4 November 2011 (Barry Popik, “The thing about smart people is that they seem like crazy people to dumb people,” The Big Apple, barrypopik.com). The line is reproduced as an anonymous online comment in Robert Todd Carroll, Unnatural Acts: Critical Thinking, Skepticism, and Science Exposed! (2012), 138. No source for it exists in Stephen Hawking’s published or recorded words.

misattribution.heading: A magnet-name credit added two years late
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most-shared “Hawking” quotes, and the citation record shows the line was already circulating with no author at all before his name was ever attached to it.

items.why: The line appears in none of Hawking’s books, lectures or documented interviews, and Wikiquote’s Hawking page ↗ does not list it under Quotes, Attributed or Misattributed. Barry Popik ↗ states there is no evidence he originated the saying or even said it, and dates the first Hawking credit to a Twitter post of 7 October 2013 — nearly two years after the line’s earliest citation on 4 November 2011.

On 5 November 2011, the day after the earliest citation, a Twitter user posted the line explicitly credited to “Unknown author,” per Popik’s citation trail ↗. That is still the most accurate credit anyone has offered.

Abraham’s line in The Walking Dead, Vol. 9 ↗ runs the same joke in far coarser language, and the volume was published on 7 January 2009 ↗, before any citation for the polite version. The wording is not the same and no quotation researcher has connected the two, so we record it as a parallel, not as the source.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who wrote it: the earliest citation on record is an unattributed tweet of 4 November 2011, and a 2012 skeptics’ book reproduces it as something “one commenter posted” (Barry Popik ↗).

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Hawking
lead: The saying arrived on the internet with no author at all. In the citation record it simply appears — a one-line Twitter aphorism on 4 November 2011 — and the following day someone was already posting it credited to “Unknown author.” By 2012 the skeptic Robert Todd Carroll could quote it in a book as something “one commenter posted,” which is exactly what it was.

Hawking’s name arrived nearly two years later, in October 2013. It is an unusually good fit for the joke, which is precisely the problem: a line about brilliance being mistaken for madness sounds right in the mouth of the man who talked about imaginary time and exploding black holes. Attribution to a famous scientist is what turned a throwaway remark into a poster, and posters do not carry footnotes.
context.pull: It began life as a comment, not a pronouncement — and spent two years with no author before Hawking’s name was attached.

sourcesVerified.claim: Barry Popik's entry on this exact saying states there is no evidence Stephen Hawking originated or said it; lists an unattributed Twitter post of 4 November 2011 (@SecularAdvocate) as the earliest citation; lists a 5 November 2011 post crediting 'Unknown author'; lists Robert Carroll's 'Unnatural Acts' (2012, p. 138) reproducing it as 'One commenter posted the following'; and dates the first Hawking-credited post to 7 October 2013, with further Hawking credits in April 2014 and after.

Wikiquote's Stephen Hawking page contains sections titled Quotes, Attributed, Misattributed, Quotes about Hawking and External links, and does not contain this line or the words 'crazy people to dumb people' in any of them.
Goodreads hosts the line credited to Stephen Hawking with no book or source listed, under the site's disclaimer that quotes are added by the community and not verified by Goodreads.
Goodreads records a coarser structurally identical line from Robert Kirkman's 'The Walking Dead, Vol. 9: Here We Remain', tagged to the character Abraham.
'The Walking Dead, Vol. 9: Here We Remain' by Robert Kirkman and Charlie Adlard was first published 7 January 2009 and collects issues #49-54.

'Unnatural Acts: Critical Thinking, Skepticism, and Science Exposed!' is by Robert Todd Carroll, published by the James Randi Educational Foundation in 2011, and is a critical-thinking/skepticism book hosted on The Skeptic's Dictionary site.
Stephen Hawking was born 8 January 1942 in Oxford and died 14 March 2018 in Cambridge; he was Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge 1979-2009 and wrote 'A Brief History of Time' (1988).
A single-quote Goodreads page reproduces the Walking Dead Vol. 9 line verbatim and credits it to Robert Kirkman with the character tag 'abraham'.
